Growing up I lived in a small town in Ohio, surrounded by nothing but cornfields and farms. When I was little I would stand out for the bus and hear the shrieks and screams of animals being slaughtered daily. It was unnerving as an 8 year old, but as I grew older I got used to it. The thing about these farms is that they never sold their meat to locals, only to corporations. Local butcheries or meat shops weren’t a thing and my parents found a side project with that.

When I was 10 we started raising our own meat. We had piggies, cows, lamb, goats, and chickens. The local community really took a liking to our animals and business was taking off. My parents let little kids come and pet the animals while the adults ate their parents. Being that we spent most of our money on animals and animal care, we didn’t really have any extra money to hire workers. At the age of 10 I learned how to butcher animals. Well, all the animals except the cows. We carved up calves and cows for meat, but my parents told me they were too intricate for me to learn. I never questioned it because why would I even want to carve up baby cows?

As time went on not only did I butcher the meat, I also became kind of an in house chef. Starting at 12 I cooked food for local people to try, and surprisingly they enjoyed it! What started out as a 12 year old girl giving her neighbors potential poison traps turned into me cooking a menu for anyone who asked. I started my passion for cooking pretty early and became very seasoned on how to make basic things. Locals thought it was pretty cute to have a sixth grader cook for them, most were weary though. Everyone’s favorite dish was the veal chops with mushrooms, I served that on such a heavy basis my family started to get worried about having beef around. Despite being a vegetarian I was pretty well versed with working with meat. Business was booming, yet some of our customers started to get sick and would disappear. That wasn’t very great on the little shop we had, but most people weren’t phased. I stopped cooking out of fear of helping these people get sick and went back to only helping out with butchering the animals.

When I turned 27 my parents had both died of an unknown brain parasite that ate holes through their brain. Doctors said it was probably because of eating infected meat and immediately I felt guilty. I had killed my parents by serving them meat that was undercooked and infected. I was the reason that people had started getting sick. I was the reason my family died. I was the reason that people around me had been dying as well. No one would blame a 12 year old girl, so I wasn’t worried about that. I was empty inside knowing what I caused. I promised my dead family that I would continue their business and vowed to never make anyone sick again.

I continued their business after I studied in a culinary school. I couldn’t allow myself to harm anyone else with my carelessness so I took steps to prevent that. The shop still had loyal customers coming and our range of meats was still the same. Despite not knowing how to butcher a cow or calf, I learned very quickly. It really wasn’t as hard as my parents had once told me, especially compared to the other animals. Business started picking up quickly and I stumbled upon the problem I had experienced when I was little, too much veal, not enough beef. I couldn’t afford more cows, or even afford to have around dairy cows to raise. I began searching around my parents house for any tips they might have left behind. >“Emily, When the time comes that you can’t afford your meat, call this number (769)-975-9076 and tell them who you are. They will deliver meats to you no questions asked.”
